description:
I have always been intrigued by this particular tree with multiple complex and convoluted trunks, and partly exposed root system. As a boy, I thought that water snakes lived in caves among the roots and could launch themselves like arrows down into the water. I'm not sure what I saw that made me believe that - perhaps leaping frogs that I didn't get a good look at. Still, it has always seemed an unusually magical place. We found the complete skeleton of a cow up above the stream bank, which we were told had been shot by someone during hunting season years before. It was fun to reassemble that skeleton back in the big barn, especially getting all the vertebrae into the right order. 

I was surprised to learn now that this might be a Basswood or Linden Tree - something interesting and even exotic sounding for around here - much less familiar than the Maples and Walnuts that are so common. 

There are a lot of Black Walnuts in their preferred riparian environment on the banks of this small creek, along with Black Willow, Shagbark Hickory, Black Cherry, and Black Maple (that I know of so far). American Sycamores are for some reason absent from this end of the valley, but abundant a mile or so downstream.

This Basswood, and maybe a few more like it, are in the valley bottom right next to this stream that is the easternmost tributary of Buffalo Creek, here at an elevation around 342 meters (1122 feet). These pasture filled valleys in the Allegheny Plateau are surrounded by rolling hills roughly 60-90 meters (200-300 feet) high covered in Appalachian mixed mesophytic deciduous (Maple-Oak-Beech) woodland. The Buffalo Creek watershed is still around 80% forested.
